name: David Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can give me the public version and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a buyer at Harbourline Foods, a regional grocery wholesaler. I buy canned tomatoes, pasta, cooking oil and the like from about 140 suppliers, and I've done it for 31 years. Mornings are phone calls and emails with sales reps, afternoons I'm in the spreadsheet working out what to order for the stores we supply. What wears me out is the squeeze: the supermarkets want lower prices every quarter and the suppliers want more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. We've had revolutions before, barcodes, EDI, the cloud, and each one just meant more screens to look at. I'd tell my mates at the allotment that the software firms oversold it, as usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm relieved, but I'm not calm. Harbourline's margins are thin and the owners keep talking about a cost review. My pay is good for this job, and that makes me a line on someone's sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing new, really. I'd keep ringing my suppliers, because I trust a voice more than a portal. I'd keep paying into my pension and plan to finish at 62 or 63. Marta, my partner, retires at 60, so we've already got a trip to Portugal pencilled in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly steady, a bit bored if I'm honest. It's the world I know and I can do it blindfolded. The only knot is the cost review, which I'd feel whichever way AI went.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the cost review. What would happen to your own job if the owners did cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd look at the people near retirement on the highest pay, and that's me. A package would probably be offered, and with our savings I'd take it and not argue. I'd just want our staff union to read the small print, because owners like to sneak in a gag clause.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you trust a voice more than a portal. Can you give me a recent example?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last spring the olive oil price jumped 20 percent. The portal said take it or leave it, so I rang Vittorio at our Spanish supplier, who I've known 15 years, and he held us at 8 percent. A handshake price beats a portal price every time.

say: I'd say AI is **overhyped** and we've seen this film before.
I'd tell colleagues that good buying still runs on **relationships**, not software.
think: I'm relieved, but the owners' **cost review** worries me more than any machine.
My high pay for the job makes me an obvious name on a **savings** list.
do: Keep **phoning** suppliers and holding my price deals by voice.
Carry on paying into my **pension** and aim to finish at 62 or 63.
Take a **package** if the owners offer one, after the union checks it.
feel: Steady and a little bored, with one **knot** about the cost review.
S0.quote: A handshake price beats a portal price every time.
fieldNote: David's worry is the employer's **cost review**, not AI itself; he already carries that pressure.
He trusts **people** over software and tells a precise story about his Spanish supplier.
Strong savings mean he would take a package calmly, so unease rather than anxiety.

steps.text: Keep phoning my 140 suppliers for price deals instead of using portals
Take a package if Harbourline offers one, after the union checks it
Keep paying into my pension while planning to finish at 62 or 63

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where the owners get their excuse. 'Software does the checking now' is how they'll sell every redundancy. I'd say it loud in our union meetings, because buyers are exactly the sort of job they mean.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think half my week goes to software within three years. The reorder calculations, the price checks, the supplier emails, all of it. Harbourline already put in a tool last year that suggests orders, and I just override it, but I can't override it forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd fight for our team to be retrained, not replaced, and I'd go to every union meeting. I'd hold off learning the new tool for as long as I decently can, then learn only what I need. Marta says that's stubbornness and she's probably right. I'd also bring my finish date forward to 61.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it makes my stomach tight. I've given this place 31 years and I can see it being turned into a button. I'm not frightened for the mortgage, I'm frightened of being pushed out of Harbourline like old furniture after 31 years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two younger buyers, Anya and Cal. When someone leaves they aren't replaced, and the work lands on the rest of us. They're 30 and 34, with kids and loans, and they're the ones who'll lose out first. I'd be angry on their behalf, more than my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd bring your finish date forward. What would you need to see before you did?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the early retirement, and quickly, if my savings hold. We've got about two years of living costs in the bank plus the house. I wouldn't sit around waiting to be told it's my turn. I'd rather leave on my terms and do some volunteering at Marta's school library.

say: I'd say **owners** will use software as the excuse for every redundancy.
I'd push at **union** meetings for retraining rather than replacement.
think: I think half of my buying week moves to **software** within three years.
I'm afraid of being pushed out like **furniture** after 31 years.
do: Go to every **union** meeting and argue for retraining of our team.
Learn only the minimum of the new **ordering tool** I must.
Bring my finish date forward to **61** if the cuts start.
feel: Tight in the stomach, and **angry** for the younger buyers more than for myself.
S1.quote: I'm not frightened for the mortgage, I'm frightened of being pushed out of Harbourline like old furniture after 31 years.
fieldNote: The money is fine, so his anxiety is about **dignity** and being pushed out, which he says plainly.
He carries concern for younger colleagues Anya and Cal, which is a different kind of worry from his own.
Resistant to the tool but already planning an exit, which shows the stubbornness has a practical backstop.

steps.text: Argue at union meetings for retraining of the buying team, not job cuts
Learn only the parts of the new ordering tool I must use
Bring my finish date forward from 63 to 61

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say nobody asked workers and nobody's ready. Two years is a joke. I'd say the government has to step in with income support and a say for unions before the whole thing lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job is gone in two years or less. Buying is checking, comparing and haggling by numbers, and a machine that thinks better than me does that for nothing. The phone calls with Vittorio might survive a year longer, but that's sentiment, not a business case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd retire the moment Harbourline lets me, which means asking for the package this winter. We have the savings and the house, and Marta can go at 60. I'd write to our MP, join a demonstration with the union, and put some money aside for the kids, because I think their jobs are the ones really in danger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sad, mostly, and a bit sick. I'm not scared for us, we'd cope. I'm scared watching my children's whole generation get walked into a wall while the owners cheer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your children about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My son Tom is an engineer and my daughter Hanna works in marketing. Both are thinking-work jobs, so both are in the line of fire two years from now. I'd tell them to save hard and stay close to us, and I'd offer the spare room if either loses a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd take action with the union. What exactly would you ask for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd press the union to ask for shorter weeks with the same pay, and a levy on firms that replace people. It may be naive. But if I do nothing I'll be sitting in the garden watching it happen, and I couldn't stand that.

say: I'd say **two years** is a joke and the government must act now.
I'd call for **income support** and a union say before the change lands.
think: My buying job is **gone** within two years, even if the phone calls last a bit longer.
My real fear is for my **children's** whole generation, not for us.
do: Ask Harbourline for the **package** this winter and retire.
Write to my **MP** and march with the union.
Put money aside for **Tom and Hanna** and keep the spare room ready.
feel: Sad and a bit **sick**, mostly for my children's sake.
S2.quote: I'm not scared for us, we'd cope. I'm scared watching my children's whole generation get walked into a wall while the owners cheer.
fieldNote: He expects to lose the job within **two years** and says so without softening it.
His distress comes from his **children's** thinking-work jobs, not his own savings.
He turns to collective action and politics, consistent with his progressive, union-first outlook.

steps.text: Ask Harbourline for a retirement package this winter
March with the union and write to my MP about income support
Put money aside for Tom and Hanna and keep the spare room ready
Push the union for shorter weeks and a levy on firms replacing staff

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, I'd say it's a warning shot. It gives us time to get laws, retraining funds and union agreements in place, if people actually use it. I'd say that to the union, and online I'd say it's the time to organise, not to panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be 63 by then with my pension in hand. I'd be retired before it bites, and that makes me feel guilty, because the buyers ten years behind me won't have my savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work another two or three years, no more, and use them to get our staff association to negotiate. I'd save as hard as I can for the kids' sake and pay off the last of the mortgage. I'd also start my volunteering early, so that I've got something to retire into.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steadier than the two-year one. Five years feels like something you can plan around, like a long winter. I'd still lie awake some nights, but mostly about other people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about most in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anya and Cal again, and the girls on the supplier-accounts desk. They've got 25 years left to work and no obvious next move. I'd ask the firm to fund a course for them now, while there's money, and I'd put my own name on the letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd feel guilty. Can you say more about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd be gone before it matters. I'd rather say it honestly than pretend I'm in the same boat as them. My use would be as a loud voice at the union and as someone who knows where the owners hide the money.

say: I'd say five years is a **warning shot** and the time to organise.
I'd tell the union to use the time to win **retraining** funds.
think: I'd be **retired** by then, so I feel guilty rather than safe.
Colleagues ten years behind me don't have my **cushion**.
do: Work two or three more years and help the staff association **negotiate**.
Pay off the last of the **mortgage** and save for the kids.
Sign a letter asking Harbourline to fund **courses** for younger buyers.
feel: Steadier than in the two-year world, but with some **guilt**.
S3.quote: I'd be retired before it bites, and that makes me feel guilty, because the buyers ten years behind me won't have my savings.
fieldNote: Five years gives him room to plan, but his remaining **working years** sit inside the change.
His guilt about being cushioned is a distinct and honest strand.
He turns that guilt into collective action for younger colleagues.

steps.text: Work two or three more years while helping the staff association negotiate
Pay off the last of the mortgage and save for the kids
Sign a letter asking Harbourline to fund courses for younger buyers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd say we can sort this out properly. I'd say schools should start teaching people how to work alongside machines, and governments should have a plan before the day arrives. Online I'd probably moan that no one in charge is doing anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it doesn't touch my own job at all, I'll be 68 and long gone. What it touches is my pension's value and my kids' careers. I'd be uneasy, but not for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working to 63 as planned, retire, and then use the free time. I'd volunteer in Marta's school library and join the union's retired section so I can keep pushing. I'd also help Tom and Hanna each work out a second skill, maybe a trade, as insurance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm, if I'm honest. Ten years is a long time, and I've seen enough bad predictions to doubt the date anyway. The worry sits at the back, like a leaky roof I'll deal with eventually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your daughter, concretely, in the first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My daughter's marketing job is the one. If she saw it coming in time, she could study to be a counsellor or a teacher. I'd push her, gently, in the first year, and offer to pay for it from our savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you doubt the date. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every prediction I've ever read had a date on it, and the date always moved. Still, ten years is enough to be sensible, so long as we start.

say: I'd say ten years is enough to build a proper **plan** if we start.
I'd say schools should teach people to work alongside **machines**.
think: It doesn't touch my own job, but it touches **Hanna's** career and my pension's value.
I doubt the **date**, because predictions have a way of moving.
do: Work to **63** as planned, then volunteer at Marta's school library.
Join the union's **retired** section to keep pushing for a plan.
Offer to pay for **Hanna** to retrain towards counselling or teaching.
feel: Fairly **calm**, with a worry at the back like a leaky roof.
S4.quote: Every prediction I've ever read had a date on it, and the date always moved. Still, ten years is enough to be sensible, so long as we start.
fieldNote: Ten years puts his own job **out of reach**, so his unease is entirely about his children and his pension.
He is **sceptical** about dates but treats the risk seriously.
Offers concrete help, paying for his daughter's retraining, rather than general hope.

steps.text: Work to 63 as planned, then volunteer in Marta's school library
Join the union's retired section to keep pushing for a plan
Offer to pay for Hanna to retrain towards counselling or teaching

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Not for me, I'd be out of the door with a package. It's the speed, because there's no way anyone organises schools, unions or governments in that time. What would help is a proper income guarantee agreed beforehand, and a legal duty on firms to talk to workers before they replace anyone.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'm not against the machines, I just don't think the people who own them should keep all the gain. If that were sorted, I'd happily watch the tomatoes order themselves.

headlineQuote: I'm not against the machines, I just don't think the people who own them should keep all the gain.
portrait: David is **58**, a wholesale buyer of canned and dry goods at Harbourline Foods, with 31 years in the trade.
He's a union man who trusts **phone calls** and old supplier relationships more than portals or software.
His savings are strong, so his fear is about being pushed out and about his **children's** jobs, not about money.
He moves from unease in the mild worlds to anger and early **retirement** plans when the change is fast.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world, because no union or government can respond in time.
whatWouldHelp: A **guarantee** of income agreed beforehand and a legal duty to consult workers.
